chapters.title: Chapter 1: Thinking Like a Hedger, Not a Trader

lessons.title: What You Are Actually Protecting Against: Drawdowns, Timing, and Goal Risk

children.text: Between 14 January and 23 March 2020, the Nifty 50 fell from about 12,362 to 7,610 on a closing basis. That is a fall of roughly 38% in ten weeks. By November 2020 it was back above its old high. So was March 2020 a disaster or a blip? It depends entirely on who you were. For a 28-year-old running a ₹15,000 SIP, it was a sale. For a 59-year-old who planned to redeem ₹40 lakh that April to retire, it was a genuine catastrophe. Same index, same fall, completely different damage. Before you spend a single rupee on protection, you need to know which of those two investors you are, and what exactly you are protecting.

body.text: Volatility is not the enemy. A market fall only becomes real damage when it is too deep to recover from in time, arrives at the wrong moment, or pushes a goal out of reach. A hedge is only worth paying for when it protects against one of those three.

children.text: Risk 1: Drawdowns and the Maths of Getting Back

markDefs.definition: The percentage fall in a portfolio or index from its previous peak to a subsequent low, before a new peak is reached.

children.text: is the fall from a peak to a trough. The trap is that losses and gains are not symmetric. If your ₹10 lakh portfolio falls 50% to ₹5 lakh, a 50% gain only takes you back to ₹7.5 lakh. You need 100% just to break even. The deeper the hole, the steeper the climb out.

body.caption: L = drawdown as a decimal. A 40% fall: 0.40 ÷ 0.60 = 0.667, so a 66.7% gain is needed.
The recovery gain needed grows much faster than the loss
headers: Years to recover at 12% a year

body.title: Gain needed to recover from a drawdown

body.text: This curve is why hedgers obsess over the left tail. Cutting a 10% fall to 7% barely matters. Cutting a 50% fall to 20% is the difference between a six-year recovery and a two-year one. Protection earns its cost in the deep drawdowns, not the everyday wobbles.

body.title: Three Nifty 50 drawdowns every Indian investor should know (approximate closing levels)

events.title: Global financial crisis: down about 60%
events.description: The Nifty fell from about 6,287 to about 2,524. It first closed above the old high in late 2010, but did not stay above it for good until 2014.

events.title: COVID crash: down about 38%
events.description: From about 12,362 to 7,610 in roughly ten weeks, the fastest deep fall in the index's history. A new high came by November 2020.

events.title: Post-peak correction: down about 16%
events.description: From a closing high of about 26,216 to near 22,000. Midcap and smallcap indices fell considerably harder, which hurt many mutual fund portfolios more than the Nifty headline suggests.

body.title: Recovery maths
body.textWithBlank: If a portfolio falls 25%, it needs a gain of about ___% to get back to where it started. (Round to the nearest whole number.)
body.explanation: 0.25 ÷ 0.75 = 0.333, so a 33% gain is needed. ₹10 lakh falls to ₹7.5 lakh, and ₹7.5 lakh × 1.333 = ₹10 lakh.

children.text: Risk 2: Timing, or When the Fall Arrives

markDefs.definition: The risk that poor returns arrive just before or during the period when you are withdrawing money, permanently reducing what you end up with, even if average returns are unchanged.

children.text: If you never withdraw, the order of returns does not matter. Multiplication does not care about sequence: −30%, +15%, +15% ends in the same place as +15%, +15%, −30%. The moment you start taking money out, that stops being true. This is
, and it is the risk that hurts retirees most.

Take two retired schoolteachers in Chennai, Mr Iyer and Mrs Nair. Each has ₹1 crore in equity funds and withdraws ₹8 lakh at the start of every year to live on. Both earn exactly the same three annual returns, just in a different order.

body.caption: Same returns, different order, ₹8 lakh withdrawn at the start of each year (₹ lakh, illustrative)

body.title: Portfolio value with withdrawals: crash first vs crash last

children.text: Mrs Nair ends with about ₹7.74 lakh more than Mr Iyer, with identical returns. Mr Iyer's crash hit when his corpus was largest, and he kept selling units at depressed prices to fund his withdrawals. Those units were never there to enjoy the recovery. This is why the years just before and just after retirement are when protection is most valuable, and why a 25-year-old SIP investor has almost no sequence risk at all.

body.title: Where you are in your investing life changes what a fall means

columns.label: Accumulating (early to mid career)
points: Corpus is small compared with future SIPs
A fall lets new SIPs buy more units at lower prices
Long runway to recover from even a deep drawdown
Main danger is behavioural: stopping SIPs or selling in panic
Paying for options protection is rarely worth the cost

columns.label: Near a goal or withdrawing (pre-retirement, retired, goal due soon)
points: Corpus is large and future contributions are small or zero
Withdrawals force selling units at low prices
Little time left to wait for a recovery
A deep fall can permanently shrink the goal
Protection, through options or asset allocation, has real value

children.text: Risk 3: Goal Risk, the One That Actually Matters

Drawdowns and timing are abstract until you tie them to a rupee amount on a date. Goal risk asks one blunt question: how far can my portfolio fall before I miss something I cannot postpone? A child's college admission, a flat's final payment, the first year of retirement expenses. That number is your tolerable drawdown, and it is the single most useful input for any hedging decision.

body.caption: The largest fall your portfolio can take and still fully fund the goal

children.text: Sanjay, 52, runs a pharma distribution business in Ahmedabad. He has ₹35 lakh in equity mutual funds and needs ₹30 lakh for his daughter's wedding in eight months. His tolerable drawdown is 1 − 30 ÷ 35 = 14.3%. A 10% fall leaves him at ₹31.5 lakh, uncomfortable but fine. A 20% fall, which the Nifty has delivered many times, leaves him at ₹28 lakh and ₹2 lakh short, with no time to wait.

stats.label: Tolerable drawdown
stats.context: Any fall beyond this means a shortfall

body.text: Notice what the tolerable drawdown gives you: a number to hedge against. In Lesson 4 of this chapter, you will see how it points directly to the strike price you should consider. An investor who has not worked out this number cannot sensibly choose a strike, and ends up buying whatever protection looks cheap.

body.title: Find the tolerable drawdown
body.prompt: Kavitha, a 49-year-old doctor in Kochi, holds ₹48 lakh in equity funds. She must pay ₹42 lakh for her son's medical college fees and hostel costs over the next 12 months. What is her tolerable drawdown, in percent?
body.explanation: 1 − 42 ÷ 48 = 1 − 0.875 = 0.125, or 12.5%. The Nifty fell about 16% between September 2024 and March 2025, so a correction of that size would have left Kavitha short. Her risk is real and specific.

children.text: The Hidden Fourth Risk: Your Own Reaction

For long-term investors with no near-term goal, the biggest damage from a crash is usually self-inflicted. Selling at the bottom in March 2020, or pausing SIPs during the 2024 to 2025 correction, turned temporary paper losses into permanent ones. Some investors find that a modest hedge helps them sit tight because they know their worst case is capped. That can be a legitimate reason to hedge, but be honest about it. If you would stay invested anyway, you are paying for comfort you do not need. If a hedge is the only thing stopping you from panic selling, a lower equity allocation may serve you better and cost nothing in premium.

body.title: Who needs protection most?
body.question: All four investors hold mainly Nifty 50 index funds. Who has the strongest case for hedging against a sharp fall over the next six months?
options: Aditya, 26, ₹3 lakh portfolio, ₹20,000 monthly SIP, no withdrawals planned for 25 years.
Farah, 41, ₹60 lakh portfolio, ₹50,000 monthly SIP, retirement target at 58.
Mr Rao, 59, ₹1.2 crore portfolio, retiring in five months and planning to withdraw ₹9 lakh a year from it.
Neha, 34, ₹18 lakh portfolio, saving for a house down payment she expects to make in about eight years.
body.explanation: Mr Rao has a large corpus, no future SIPs to average down, withdrawals starting almost immediately, and heavy sequence risk. A deep fall now would directly shrink his retirement income. Aditya actually benefits from falls. Farah and Neha have years to recover before they need the money.

body.title: Define the risk before choosing the tool
body.scenario: Deepak, 57, is a senior engineer at a PSU in Bhopal. He has ₹80 lakh in equity mutual funds, mostly flexi-cap and midcap funds, and ₹25 lakh in PPF and FDs. He retires in 14 months. His plan is to move ₹30 lakh into an SCSS and debt funds at retirement to cover his first five years of expenses. He is nervous after reading that valuations are stretched and asks you whether he should start buying Nifty puts.
body.prompt: Before talking about options at all, identify Deepak's real risks using the three risks from this lesson. What is his tolerable drawdown for the money he needs, and what questions should he answer first?
body.modelAnswer:
1. Goal risk: he needs ₹30 lakh from his equity funds in 14 months. His tolerable drawdown on the equity portfolio is 1 − 30 ÷ 80 = 62.5%, so he is extremely unlikely to fall short of the ₹30 lakh itself.
2. Timing and sequence risk: this is his real exposure. A 30% fall just before retirement would cut his equity corpus from ₹80 lakh to ₹56 lakh. After moving ₹30 lakh out, only ₹26 lakh would be left to grow for the rest of his retirement, instead of ₹50 lakh.
3. Drawdown risk: his midcap-heavy funds may fall harder than the Nifty in a correction, so a Nifty hedge would only partly offset his losses. Chapter 3 covers this mismatch.
4. Questions first: Could he simply start moving the ₹30 lakh to debt in stages now? What would that cost in capital gains tax compared with the cost of puts? How much of the remaining ₹50 lakh does he truly need to protect, given his PPF, FDs and pension?
The right answer may be partly moving to debt early and possibly hedging a portion of the rest. The wrong move is buying puts on the full ₹80 lakh because he feels nervous.

body.title: Show me the math: why order does not matter without withdrawals

children.text: Without withdrawals, ₹1 crore after three years is simply ₹1 crore × each year's growth factor multiplied together:

content.caption: ₹ lakh. Multiplication gives the same answer in any order.

children.text: Both would end at about ₹92.58 lakh. A withdrawal breaks this because it is a fixed rupee amount taken out between the multiplications. Taking ₹8 lakh from a portfolio that just fell 30% removes a bigger share of it than taking ₹8 lakh from one that just rose 15%.

body.title: Name your risk before you hedge it
steps: Write down every goal that will need money from your equity portfolio in the next three years, with the rupee amount and date.
Calculate your tolerable drawdown for the nearest goal using 1 minus amount needed divided by portfolio value.
Note whether you are still adding money through SIPs, or have started or are about to start withdrawing.
Look up how much your actual funds fell between September 2024 and March 2025, not just the Nifty.
Ask whether the risk is temporary (a goal due soon) or permanent (simply too much equity for your stage of life).

cards.definition: The percentage fall from a previous peak to a subsequent low.
The gain needed to get back to the old peak after a fall: L ÷ (1 − L). A 50% fall needs a 100% gain.
The damage caused when poor returns arrive just as withdrawals begin, even if average returns are unchanged.
The risk that a market fall leaves you short of money needed for a specific goal on a specific date.
The largest fall a portfolio can take and still fully fund a goal: 1 − amount needed ÷ portfolio value.
The risk that you sell or stop investing in a panic, turning a temporary fall into a permanent loss.

points: A market fall only matters if it is too deep, arrives at the wrong time, or breaks a goal. Hedge those, not everyday volatility.
Losses need bigger gains to recover: 20% needs 25%, 40% needs 66.7%, 50% needs 100%.
Sequence risk only bites once withdrawals begin, which makes the years around retirement the most dangerous.
Tolerable drawdown, 1 − amount needed ÷ portfolio value, turns a vague worry into a number you can hedge against.
Young SIP investors have little financial reason to pay for protection. Their real risk is panic.
Sometimes moving money to debt ahead of a goal protects better, and more cheaply, than any option.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Index levels are approximate closing values, and the return sequences and investor examples are illustrative. Past drawdowns do not predict future ones. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser before making changes to your portfolio.
